titleText.es: Aunque... ¿quién más no puede esperar a que incorporen en los juegos el tema ese del head-tracking con el Wiimote? Tío, el futuro va a ser *alucinante*.
titleText.en: Although ... who else can't wait for them to incorporate that Wiimote head-tracking stuff into games?  Man, the future's gonna be *awesome*.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish page's image alt text repeats only the strip title, while its separate title attribute contains the full Wiimote and head-tracking joke preserved above. The official English title text has two spaces before Man; that source spacing is preserved exactly.

regions.labelEs: ¡OHH, CREO QUE YA LO TENGO! VALE, UNA HORA MÁS.

applications.explanationEn: Lo replaces the masculine thing already understood and appears directly before the changed verb tengo.
Una gives the quantity, hora names what is counted, and más follows the noun to mark the additional amount.

regions.labelEs: LOS SISTEMAS DE JUEGOS MÁS POTENTES DEL MUNDO TODAVÍA NO PUEDEN IGUALAR LA ADICCIÓN DE LOS JUEGOS FLASH DEL NAVEGADOR.

applications.exampleEs: LOS SISTEMAS DE JUEGOS MÁS POTENTES
applications.explanationEn: Los matches the masculine plural noun sistemas, and más before potentes marks the highest degree within the group.
Potentes is plural because it describes the plural noun sistemas; the same -es plural form works with masculine and feminine nouns.
Del introduces mundo as the larger group within which the systems are being compared.
Todavía and no work together to show that the negative situation remains true up to this point.
Pueden changes for the plural subject, while igualar keeps its unchanged -ar ending as the possible action.
This occurrence uses adicción for the games' addictive quality, rather than for one particular person's dependence.

cards.noteEn: Writing extra letters stretches the spoken reaction. Here ohh shows pleased surprise at the measurement, rather than disappointment.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

cards.answerEn: one (feminine singular, before a counted noun)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun for both the number one and the indefinite article “a.” Context shows whether an exact count matters.

cards.questionEn: How do you express an additional number of things, as in ‘three more chairs’?
cards.answerEn: Put the number or amount first, then the thing being counted, and place más after it.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places más after the counted noun even though English puts ‘more’ before it: un día más is ‘one more day,’ and dos días más is ‘two more days.’ The noun changes between singular and plural to match the amount.
Hora can name a length of sixty minutes as well as a clock time. A number before it makes the measured duration clear.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe someone or something as the most of a quality?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of “the,” name the person or thing, then add más plus the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The opening el, la, los, or las agrees with the noun. Más stays unchanged, while the final adjective changes when Spanish normally requires agreement.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
Más normally means “more.” After el, la, los, or las, it can instead mark the highest degree in a group: la más rápida means “the fastest one.”
Potente has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns. Potentes is its plural form.

cards.answerEn: in the; introduces the group used for a ‘most’ or ‘least’ comparison
cards.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After a description with más or menos that picks out an extreme, it can introduce the larger group being compared. Natural English often uses ‘in the’ rather than translating de literally as ‘of.’

example.es: Es el edificio más alto del barrio.
example.en: It is the tallest building in the neighborhood.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use todavía no before the action, or alone when the action is understood.
cards.noteEn: The Spanish order literally resembles “still not,” while natural English often uses “not yet.”

cards.answerEn: they can; they are able to

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Adicción usually names an addiction or dependence. It can also point to the quality that makes an activity very hard to stop, which English can call “addictiveness.”

cards.answerEn: of; links a quality or effect to what has or causes it
cards.noteEn: De can connect a quality, feature, or effect to the thing it comes from. English usually keeps “of” or uses a possessive form.

example.es: Me sorprende la fuerza de este viento.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general group
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses los before a plural group discussed as a whole, as in los programadores. English often leaves “the” out and simply says “programmers” when making the same general statement.

cards.answerEn: They were games made with Adobe Flash that ran inside a web browser, usually through a small browser add-on called a plug-in.
cards.noteEn: Flash supported animation, sound, and interaction, so it became a common platform for quick web games before modern browser technologies replaced it. Adobe ended support for Flash Player in 2020.

example.es: Muchos juegos Flash se abrían desde una página web.
example.en: Many Flash games opened from a web page.

cards.noteEn: Flash is the unchanged name of an older multimedia platform. In a phrase such as juegos Flash, it identifies the technology used to make or run the games.

example.es: El museo conserva una animación Flash.
example.en: The museum preserves a Flash animation.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.noteEn: Navegador can describe a navigator, but in computing it commonly means a web browser: the program used to open websites.

example.es: Abre el enlace en el navegador.
example.en: Open the link in the web browser.
